u576: God tenderly describes Himself caring for mothers: "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd... and shall gently lead those that are with young" (Isaiah 40:11). He knows Deepa's season. Paul encourages us to "pray without ceasing" (1 Thessalonians 5:17), which suggests ongoing conversation rather than one perfect hour. The widow's small offering pleased Jesus more than large gifts (Mark 12:43-44). God values the heart, not the size. Lamentations reminds us, "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning" (Lamentations 3:22-23). Each morning is a fresh invitation, even if it is just five minutes.
u577: God designed the brain to build habits through small repeated actions linked to cues. A tiny routine repeated daily can rewire the brain more powerfully than an occasional long effort. He made seasons of life with different capacities, and He understands the exhaustion of caring for small children. Our brains also respond to grace and encouragement, which make good habits easier. God designed relationship to grow through regular contact, so even brief daily moments with Him keep connection alive.
u578: Isaiah 40:11|and shall gently lead those that are with young
u582: Deepa kept her five minutes on most mornings for three months. Some days the baby screamed and she only managed one sentence, and she learned that was alright. Her children began joining her verse at breakfast. When the baby started sleeping better, her five minutes sometimes grew to fifteen. She no longer feels like a failure, but like a daughter.
u583: In busy seasons, a tiny, consistent habit with God is better than waiting for a perfect hour.
u584: Deepa was too busy for a long prayer time. So she talked to God for five minutes while making tea, and it helped her feel close to Him.
u585: Rohit and the game that came before everything
u586: Rohit, 19, an engineering student in Indore who loves online games
u587: Rohit plays online games most nights until two or three in the morning. He always manages to submit urgent assignments, usually at the last minute, so he thinks he is doing fine. But he skips everything that does not have a deadline. He never revises for exams until the night before, has stopped going to the gym, rarely calls his parents and has not been to church since he moved to the hostel. He promised himself he would learn coding outside the syllabus to get a good job, but he has not started. When he thinks about these things, they seem boring or far away, while his game team needs him tonight. His grades are average and he feels a vague emptiness. Recently his friend got an internship through a coding project, and Rohit felt a sharp pang of regret.
u588: Research suggests the brain values immediate, certain rewards over distant ones, a pattern called temporal discounting. Games are designed with constant rewards, levels and social belonging, so they win easily over coding or revision. Deadlines create urgency that forces action, but important tasks without deadlines never feel urgent. Late nights weaken his prefrontal cortex, making self-control even harder. The game team also meets his need for belonging and competence, which explains why he chooses it. Spiritually, being far from home and church has cut him off from relationships that once supported his faith.
u589: His regret over the internship became a turning point. He wrote down what really mattered to him in five years: a good job, health, a close relationship with God and his family. He realised that none of these could be achieved by deadlines alone. He asked a classmate to learn coding together.
u590: Write his top values and goals clearly
u591: Schedule important tasks like urgent ones, with fixed times
u592: Limit gaming to weekends or two hours on weeknights
u593: Code with a friend three evenings a week
u594: Join a Christian fellowship near the hostel
u596: Paul writes, "See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time" (Ephesians 5:15-16). Moses prayed, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psalm 90:12). Jesus warned that cares and pleasures can choke the word (Luke 8:14). Paul also said, "All things are lawful unto me, but I will not be brought under the power of any" (1 Corinthians 6:12). Games are not evil, but they should not rule Rohit. God invites him to choose what matters most, not out of fear, but because his life is a gift.
u597: God designed us to enjoy play, challenge and teamwork, which are good gifts. He also gave us the ability to think about the future and choose long-term goals. When the reward system is constantly stimulated by fast pleasures, the brain struggles to value slower, deeper rewards. God made us to need rest, so sleep restores self-control. He also designed us for meaningful work and relationship, which bring deeper joy than quick wins.
u598: Psalm 90:12|So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
u602: Rohit cut his gaming to weekends and two nights a week. Some weeks he still binged during holidays. But his coding project with his friend is growing, and he applied for an internship. He joined a hostel Bible study and calls his parents on Sundays. He sleeps better, and the emptiness has eased.
u603: What is urgent or fun often crowds out what truly matters unless we deliberately make room for it.
u604: Rohit played games all night and only did homework when it was due. When he planned time for important things, his life got better.
u605: Mr. Gopal and the phone he was afraid to touch
u606: Gopal, 71, a retired railway clerk in Bhubaneswar
u607: When Gopal's grandson gave him a smartphone, he smiled politely and put it back in the box. His old keypad phone was enough, he said. But now his church streams services online, his doctor sends reports by message, and his daughter in Canada wants video calls. Each time someone tries to teach him, they tap the screen quickly, say "just do this, Appa" and walk away. He presses the wrong button, something pops up, and he panics that he has broken it. He feels foolish and old. He tells everyone he is not interested in these new things. Secretly, he feels left behind and lonely. He misses seeing his granddaughter's face and the Sunday sermons. He watches his friends confidently using phones and wonders whether his mind has become too slow.
u608: Research suggests that older adults can learn new skills well, especially with patient, step-by-step teaching. Gopal's fear of breaking the phone and looking foolish activates the stress system, which makes it harder to remember steps. Fast, impatient teaching overwhelms working memory. He has a fixed mindset belief that old people cannot learn technology. Avoidance protects his dignity but deepens loneliness. Spiritually, he has quietly believed his useful years are over.
u609: His granddaughter, visiting for summer, sat with him slowly and wrote each step in a notebook in Odia, with drawings of the buttons. She let him press everything himself, and reassured him he could not break it by tapping wrongly. He laughed when his first video call worked.
u610: Learn one task at a time, such as answering a video call
u611: Write each step in his own language in a notebook
u612: Practise the same task daily for a week
u614: Celebrate each new skill with family
u615: The psalmist rejoices that the righteous "shall still bring forth fruit in old age" (Psalm 92:14). God says to the elderly, "even to your old age I am he, and even to hoar hairs will I carry you" (Isaiah 46:4). Caleb, at eighty-five, said, "As yet I am as strong this day... give me this mountain" (Joshua 14:11-12). Proverbs calls grey hair "a crown of glory" (Proverbs 16:31). Gopal's life is not over. God still has purpose for him, and learning new things can open doors to connection and ministry.
u616: God designed the brain to remain changeable throughout life. New skills form new connections, even in old age, though learning may take a little longer. Repetition, patience and emotional safety help older brains learn well. God made us for connection across generations, so that young and old can teach and learn from each other. Learning something new also keeps the brain healthy and engaged, and it reminds us that God is not finished with us at any age.
u617: Psalm 92:14|They shall still bring forth fruit in old age
u621: Over two months, Gopal learned video calls, messages and watching church online. He still calls his grandson in a panic sometimes when the screen changes. But now he sends good morning verses to his church group and video calls his daughter weekly. He is even teaching a friend from church how to do the same. He says he feels young again.
u622: With patient, step-by-step teaching, it is never too late to learn something new.
u623: Gopal was scared of his phone. His granddaughter taught him slowly, one step at a time, and now he can video call his family.
u624: Hannah and the family devotions she used to hate
u625: Hannah, 22, a pastor's daughter studying design in Mumbai
u626: Growing up, Hannah had family devotions every night at nine sharp. Her father, a pastor, read long passages, asked questions like a quiz, and scolded her if she yawned or answered wrongly. If she missed devotions for a friend's birthday, she was lectured about worldliness. People at church expected her to be perfect. By sixteen she dreaded nine o'clock. By eighteen she moved to college and stopped reading the Bible completely. She still believes in God, but the word devotion makes her stomach tighten. When friends talk about loving prayer, she feels angry and confused. She wonders whether she ever had faith of her own, or only performed it to please her parents. Part of her wants God, but another part never wants to be forced again.
u627: Research suggests that when people feel controlled, they often resist the very thing they are pushed toward, even if they value it. Hannah's devotions were linked with fear and judgement, so her brain now associates Scripture with stress. Moving away gave her autonomy for the first time, and rejecting devotions felt like freedom. She also absorbed a harsh picture of God as a strict father who checks every answer. Underneath, she longs for a faith that is truly hers. Her father loved God and her deeply, but his anxiety about her spiritual life came out as control.
u628: Hannah met a gentle older woman at a small church who asked her, "What do you think God is really like?" Hannah answered honestly, "Angry and demanding." The woman invited her to read the Gospels and simply watch how Jesus treated people. Slowly, a new picture began to form.
u629: Read one Gospel story at a time with curiosity, not pressure
u630: Ask what Jesus shows about God's heart
u631: Pray honestly, including about her anger
u632: Choose her own time and way to meet God
u633: Talk with a counsellor or mentor about her past
u634: Later, share her feelings gently with her father
u635: Jesus described God as a father who runs to meet his returning son and "had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). He also said, "I will not leave you comfortless" (John 14:18). The Lord says, "I have loved thee with an everlasting love: therefore with lovingkindness have I drawn thee" (Jeremiah 31:3). God draws, He does not drag. Jesus said, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). Hannah can discover that God is gentle, not harsh.
u636: God designed us with a deep need for autonomy, the freedom to choose. He does not force love, because true love must be freely given. When faith is pressured, the brain may link it with threat, but new experiences of grace can reshape those associations. God also designed relationships to heal, so safe mentors can help us see Him more truly. He made us to know Him personally, not just through our parents' faith.
u637: Jeremiah 31:3|with lovingkindness have I drawn thee
u641: Over a year, Hannah slowly began reading the Gospels on her own terms. Some weeks she still avoided God and felt angry. But she found herself praying on walks and enjoying worship songs again. She eventually talked with her father, who listened and apologised. Their relationship is still healing, but Hannah now says her faith is finally hers.
u642: Faith that was forced can become freely chosen love when we meet the gentle heart of God for ourselves.
u643: Hannah was forced to pray as a child and started to hate it. When she learned that Jesus is kind, she began to love God in her own way.
